proof:
# Concave buffered depth regions and their exact source response

This note proves a bounded convex-region construction proposed by root.
It preserves the actual finite mixed measure and quantifies its depth
error. Its active caps need not form an ordinary through-source positive
normal circuit. They nevertheless cover the source FIBER by a separate
concavity argument. No OC payment or perturbative continuation of a
global deepest set is asserted.

## 1. Actual canonical family and a continuous concave buffer

Let P be a nonempty finite lattice-complete subset of Z^n, and let K_z
be positive d-dimensional compact convex bodies satisfying all anchored
inclusions. Put

    C=conv union_(z in P) ({z} times K_z),
    B=conv P,   S=union_(z in P) ({z} times K_z),
    mu=sum_(z in P) delta_z times Lebesgue|K_z,  M=mu(S).

Base statements are relative to aff B. At every real z in B the fiber
C_z is full-dimensional. The abstract hypotheses on the buffer f are:
it is continuous, nonnegative and concave on ALL of C, positive in
the interior of each fiber, and zero on each fiber boundary. Sections
2--6 use precisely these hypotheses. The first important example is

    f(z,x)=T_(C_z)(x)^(1/d),

where T is the maximum density-dominated mass with centroid x. Set
T=0 when x lies on the boundary of C_z.

This f is nonnegative, continuous and concave on C. Concavity, including
containing target fibers, is the actual retained-cap coupling theorem in
`candidate 38e8cdfda56d1d3d`.
Here are the continuity details needed at base boundaries and fiber
boundaries, which concavity alone would not supply.

For each unit u, finite linear programming gives

    h_(C_z)(u)=max{sum lambda_p h_(K_p)(u):
                 lambda>=0, sum lambda=1, sum lambda p=z}.

The dual is a pointed polyhedron of affine majorants of the finitely
many heights h_(K_p)(u). Every vertex uses an independent subset of the
fixed rows (1,p). Its slope is therefore uniformly bounded as u varies,
since all heights are bounded and there are finitely many subsets.
Taking the minimum of these dual affine functions proves a uniform
Hausdorff-Lipschitz bound for C_z, including z on the boundary of B.
This is the finite support-roof argument proved in
`candidate c0fc791108fc8765`.
The real fibers have a common positive inradius: choose equal-radius
balls in the finitely many sampled fibers and interpolate their centers.

If K_j tends to a full-dimensional K in Hausdorff distance and y_j in
K_j tends to y in K, the hinge formula

    T_K(y)=inf_u integral_K [1+u.(X-y)]_+ dX

implies upper semicontinuity by testing each fixed u and passing to the
limit in its bounded continuous integral. At a boundary y this infimum
is zero: if v.(X-y)<=0 is a supporting inequality, use u=R v and let
R tend to infinity. The integrands tend to zero except on a null
supporting hyperplane. If y is interior, K-y contains r times the unit
ball. With delta_j=d_H(K_j-y_j,K-y), support functions show

    (1-delta_j/r)(K-y) subset K_j-y_j

for large j. A corresponding contracted translate of the optimal
retained cap proves lower semicontinuity. This establishes the asserted
joint continuity, including T=0 at fiber boundaries.

Two further examples are E_(C_z)(x)^(1/d) and E_(C_z)(x)^(1/(d+1)).
The first is jointly concave by the projective-energy transport theorem;
the second is its increasing concave power d/(d+1). Interior continuity
follows from attained energy minimizers, their positive denominator
floor, and the same Hausdorff fiber continuity. Boundary continuity
follows from 0<=E<=(d+1)T. Both are positive on fiber interiors and
zero on fiber boundaries. The power 1/(d+1) has a particularly exact
normalizer alignment, recorded in Section 9.

## 2. Definition, quantiles and convexity

For w=(z,x) in C and epsilon>=0 define

    b_epsilon(w)=min{ b_base(z),
       inf_(a, ||u||=1)
       mu{a.(Z-z)+u.(X-x)>=-epsilon f(w)} },             (1)

where b_base is the CLOSED weighted atomic halfspace depth for the
fiber volumes. In rank zero set b_base=M. In particular b_0 is exactly
the actual mixed halfspace depth, evaluated also at real-base points.

For 0<q<=M define the upper quantile

    c_q(a,u)=sup{c: mu{a.Z+u.X>=c}>=q}.                 (2)

For ||u||=1 the projected law is absolutely continuous and compactly
supported, hence has a continuous tail: each fiber contributes a
one-dimensional coarea density, which need not be continuous at its
support endpoints.
It can have gaps, so use the RIGHT endpoint in (2); no strict quantile
inverse is presumed. Continuity of its tail gives the exact equivalence

    mu{a.Z+u.X>=s}>=q   iff   s<=c_q(a,u).              (3)

For pure-base directions use the same definition with their atomic
closed tails. The set where the tail is at least q is still a closed
initial interval, so the analogous equivalence remains true even at
jumps. Its quantile constraints define the usual convex base region.

Consequently the buffered depth region is EXACTLY

    D_(q,epsilon)={w in C: b_base(z)>=q,
       a.z+u.x-epsilon f(w)<=c_q(a,u)
                        for every a and unit u}.       (4)

Every inequality in (4) is a convex sublevel inequality because f is
concave. Thus D_(q,epsilon) is compact and convex. Quantile plateaus do
not change this conclusion. No supporting halfspace is replaced by an
open one.

For fixed q, c_q is continuous in (a,u) away from u=0. Indeed a uniform
pointwise perturbation of a.Z+u.X by at most eta shifts its upper
quantile by at most eta, using (3) in both directions. Compactness of
S bounds this eta by a constant times the parameter perturbation.

## 3. Uniform original-depth error and attained buffered maxima

Let

    L=sum_(z in P) sup_(||u||=1,s in R)
                      H^(d-1)(K_z intersect {u.X=s}),
    Fmax=max_C f.

In d=1 each summand of L is one. These constants are finite: enclose
the finitely many bodies in a fixed ball and bound their sections by
the corresponding (d-1)-ball. Direct coarea integration, uniformly
over EVERY base tilt a, gives

    b_0(w)<=b_epsilon(w)<=b_0(w)+epsilon L f(w)
                          <=b_0(w)+epsilon L Fmax.       (5)

The pure-base term is unchanged. Taking an infimum preserves the two
bounds because the same additive error bounds every nonvertical cap.

For each fixed cap parameter its buffered mass is continuous in w:
the threshold is continuous and the projected law has no atom. The
pure-base closed-tail term is upper semicontinuous. Thus b_epsilon is
upper semicontinuous, and its maximum on the compact actual mixed set
S is attained. Write

    Q=max_S b_0>0,       Q_epsilon=max_S b_epsilon.

Then

    Q<=Q_epsilon<=Q+epsilon L Fmax.                    (6)

Every limit of buffered maximizing points as epsilon tends to zero is
an actual deepest point, by (5) and upper semicontinuity of b_0.

At a boundary point y of any sampled fiber K_p, b_0(p,y)=0. To check
this with the actual integer fibers, choose a continuous support normal
u at y and a finite affine support majorant touching h_(K_p)(u) at p.
The finite-hull dual construction above provides such a majorant.
Its OUTWARD ambient cap meets every fiber only in a support plane or
not at all, so has zero d-volume. Since f=0 at that point, b_epsilon=0
there as well. The compact positive-depth set {w in S:b_0(w)>=Q/2}
therefore has a uniform positive distance from every own-fiber boundary.
For small epsilon, (5) places every buffered maximizer in this set.
In particular, for all such maximizers and all unit u, the shifted
own-fiber plane at u.y-epsilon f(p,y) is proper, uniformly away from
the two supporting levels. This does not remove supporting contacts
in OTHER fibers.

## 4. Local compactification and an actual finite source balance

Fix epsilon>0, a fiberwise local maximizer w=(p,y) of b_epsilon, and
write q=b_epsilon(w). Assume

    y in int K_p,
    epsilon f(p,y)<dist(y,boundary K_p).                (7)

These conditions automatically give the strict gap q<b_base(p).
Choose a pure-base minimizing halfspace through p; it is attained
because only finitely many subsets of P can occur. Write its normal
a. For any unit u, the nonvertical cap with base tilt k a has, for
large finite k, exactly the same full/empty status on every base with
a.(z-p)>0 or <0. On the zero-drift bases it has continuous traces at
u.y-epsilon f(p,y). The own trace is proper by (7), so omits positive
volume. Thus this cap has strictly less mass than the CLOSED pure-base
minimizer. In rank zero the same assertion follows from any proper
own continuous cut. No atomic boundary fiber is silently dropped;
its positive lost continuous portion is the reason for the gap.
Section 3 supplies (7) for all small-epsilon global maximizers.

Every cap value in a neighborhood of y has a uniformly bounded tilt
representative. To see this, choose H larger than every absolute
u.(X-y')+epsilon f(p,y') in that neighborhood. For a given a keep all
a.(z-p) in [-H,H] fixed and impose the corresponding >=H or <=-H
inequality on the other evaluations. The resulting nonempty polyhedron
has a minimum-norm point. This point is orthogonal to the common kernel
of its active rows; selecting an independent active-row basis expresses
it by a fixed pseudoinverse times a vector with entries bounded by H.
There are finitely many bases of the fixed rows z-p, giving a uniform
norm bound. All proper traces are preserved exactly and all strict
full/empty statuses are preserved. Hence the cap infimum in (1) is
attained in a compact parameter set locally. This is precisely the
archived clipping/minimum-norm tilt argument; it does not presume tilt
coercivity or a bounded arbitrary original tilt.

For the convex argument define

    G_q(Y)=inf_(a,||u||=1)[c_q(a,u)-a.p-u.Y].

This function is finite near y, concave and 1-Lipschitz there. Indeed
feasibility at y bounds every affine function below at y, while any
fixed parameter bounds the infimum above; all their Y-slopes are unit.
Moreover its near-active terms admit the same compact tilt reduction.
Their own quantile lies in a fixed proper interval of K_p, by (7).
Clipping a as above preserves their cap mass q and their threshold
c_q-a.p. A proper own trace makes the tail strictly decreasing locally,
so the preserved threshold is still the RIGHT q-quantile after the
replacement. Terms separated by a fixed positive gap at y remain
irrelevant near y by the unit-slope bound. It follows that G_q locally
is the minimum over a fixed compact parameter set, and its active
normals form a compact set.

The local maximum assumption and the proper own trace give

    G_q(Y)+epsilon f(p,Y)<=0,
    G_q(y)+epsilon f(p,y)=0                             (8)

near y. If the buffered mass is below q, (3) makes the first inequality
strict. If it is q, the attained cap has a proper own trace, so its
threshold is exactly the right q-quantile. The base gap excludes the
only other bottleneck.

The superdifferential of G_q at y is the convex hull of the negatives
of its active unit normals. The sum rule for finite concave functions
on an open neighborhood, applied to the local maximum (8), gives a
supergradient g of f(p,.) at y and a convex combination of active normals
such that

    sum_j rho_j u_j=epsilon g,    rho_j>=0, sum_j rho_j=1. (9)

Caratheodory reduces this to at most d+1 active caps; zero coefficients
may be discarded. Every selected cap has ACTUAL mass q and equation

    H_j={a_j.Z+u_j.X>=a_j.p+u_j.y-epsilon f(p,y)}.      (10)

No differentiability of f or supporting-cap coarea has been used in
(9). This is a convex source optimality statement, not an unqualified
finite KKT representation of a secondary energy maximum.

## 5. What cover survives, and what ordinary circuit does not

The selected closed caps (10) cover the ENTIRE source fiber K_p.
For every X in K_p their weighted margin is

    sum_j rho_j[u_j.(X-y)+epsilon f(p,y)]
       =epsilon[f(p,y)+g.(X-y)]
       >=epsilon f(p,X)>=0.                           (11)

The first inequality is the global supergradient inequality for the
concave function f on its own fiber. Thus at least one margin is
nonnegative, including for boundary X where f vanishes. This is an
actual finite affine-cap cover, not merely a curved-constraint cover.

Nevertheless (9) does NOT assert sum rho_j u_j=0. The caps do not pass
through y: their own trace planes are shifted by epsilon f(p,y)>0.
The selected normals need not positively span the continuous space,
and the caps need not cover that WHOLE space. Ordinary through-source
positive-circuit rigidity, and any parity payment requiring it, cannot
be imported without an additional argument. Convexity of (4) and the
source-fiber cover (11) are the precise properties proved here.

## 6. Regular active quantiles give an exact section-centroid shift

Now suppose a selected active cap is regular in the following explicit
sense: its mass is C1 in the FULL hyperplane parameters (a,u,c) in a
neighborhood, and its positive total coarea S differentiates threshold
motion. The proper own trace guarantees S>0; the C1 hypothesis still
excludes unaccounted positive-area supporting contacts elsewhere.

The implicit quantile derivative is

    grad_a c_q=bar z,       grad_u c_q=bar X,

where (bar z,bar X) is the barycenter of the actual mixed section
measure, using coarea H^(d-1)/||u|| in each fiber. At ||u||=1 the latter
factor is one. Feasibility of all cap parameters and equality for the
active one makes a.p+u.y-epsilon f(p,y)-c_q locally maximal over all
a and the unit sphere u. Its normal variations give

    bar z=p,          projection_(u-perp)(bar X-y)=0.

Homogeneity of c_q, together with its active value, then gives

    bar X=y-epsilon f(p,y)u.                           (12)

This is an exact displaced section centroid. It is not the old equality
bar X=y, and it is not asserted for a nonsmooth supporting-cap branch.

## 7. Conditional physical response and the additional own-source term

First specialize f=T^(1/d). Assume the finitely selected caps in (9)
are regular as in Section 6, and that y is NOT the ordinary centroid
of K_p. Then the optimal
retained hinge is unique, say h(X)=[1+v_*.(X-y)]_+. The retained-mass
first-variation theorem in
`candidate cb7ea417552f0084`
applies to any actual compatible erosion with its bounded physical
boundary speeds v_z satisfying that theorem's radial hypotheses.
For a fixed source mark let

    C_T=integral_(boundary K_p) h(X)v_p(X)dS,
    dot f_body=-(1/d)T^(1/d-1) C_T.                    (13)

Let L_j be the actual fixed closed-cap loss of H_j under that SAME
erosion, and S_j its section coarea. Move the source at velocity w,
keeping p fixed. For the same normal parameters (a_j,u_j) the buffered
cap threshold moves at rate

    u_j.w-epsilon(dot f_body+g.w),

where g=grad_y f. Thus its actual mass derivative is

    -L_j+epsilon S_j dot f_body-S_j(u_j-epsilon g).w.  (14)

Set theta_j=(rho_j/S_j)/sum_l(rho_l/S_l). Equation (9) cancels the
mark-velocity term in the theta-weighted response. Its negative is

    sum_j theta_j L_j-epsilon(sum_j theta_j S_j)dot f_body
      =sum_j theta_j L_j
        +(epsilon/d)(sum_j theta_j S_j)T^(1/d-1)C_T.    (15)

All losses in this identity come from the original actual bodies and
the same deformation. For inward erosions the extra own-hinge term
is nonnegative. The formula is a selected-menu response identity;
it is not automatically the derivative of the globally reoptimized
buffered maximum, nor a strict normalized-mass descent certificate.
At y=g_(K_p), the hinge optimizer is not unique; the coupled minimum
formula must be retained, and (13)--(15) are not asserted unchanged.

The same weighted identity preceding (15),

    selected loss=sum theta_j L_j
                       -epsilon(sum theta_j S_j)dot f_body,      (16)

holds for any buffer differentiable in the own mark and possessing an
actual fixed-mark shape derivative. For f=E^r, r=1/d or 1/(d+1),
let a be the optimizing projective parameter and L(X)=1+a.(X-y).
At EVERY interior mark, including the ordinary centroid,

    g=r(d+1)f a,
    dot f_body=-r E^(r-1) integral_(boundary K_p)L(X)^(-d-1)v_p dS.
                                                                    (17)

Here the envelope derivative is legitimate for the same radial
erosions: the minimizers stay in a compact parameter set, converge to
the unique old minimizer, and retain a uniform positive denominator
on the old body for small erosion time. The weighted radial shell
formula has a uniform first-order expansion on that set. Evaluating
at the old minimizer for the upper derivative and at the new minimizer
for the lower derivative proves (17). The mark derivative follows
from energy stationarity and its escort identity. Thus (16) gives a
nonnegative additional own-projective-kernel term for inward erosion,
without the centroid hinge ambiguity of T.

For the length-homogeneous choices f=T^(1/d) or E^(1/d), uniformly rescaling
all continuous coordinates by s>0 and all continuous marks likewise,
while rescaling each base tilt a to s a, multiplies every buffered cap
mass and its maximum by s^d. Thus normalized buffered depth is unchanged.
For f=E^(1/(d+1)), this statement requires simultaneously replacing
epsilon by s^(1/(d+1))epsilon. A FIXED epsilon is not scale invariant
for that power; the compact-family limit epsilon->0 in (5)--(6) is
unaffected.

## 8. Full supergradients and a fixed deepest-base-face cover

For the three stated buffers a selected own-fiber supergradient g
extends to a finite full supergradient (alpha,g), even when p is on
the boundary of the base polytope. Here is a direct proof that retains
the prescribed g. Put

    phi(z)=max_(X in C_z)[f(z,X)-g.(X-y)].

This is a concave function on B and phi(p)=f(p,y). It is Lipschitz.
Indeed every fiber has a uniform inner-ball radius r_0 and is uniformly
bounded. If two fibers are at Hausdorff distance delta<r_0, contract
the first about the center of such a ball by 1-delta/r_0. Support
functions place the contraction inside the second. Under this physical
marked contraction, the relevant buffer is multiplied by
(1-delta/r_0)^kappa, where kappa is 1 for T^(1/d),E^(1/d) and
d/(d+1) for E^(1/(d+1)). Monotonicity under inclusion and boundedness
of f and g.X therefore bound the decrease of phi by C delta. Reverse
the fibers to obtain the other bound. The Hausdorff-Lipschitz fiber
estimate makes phi Lipschitz in z.

The finite convex function -phi on B has a convex Lipschitz extension
to its full affine span, namely inf_(z in B)[-phi(z)+L|w-z|] for a
Lipschitz constant L. A subgradient of this extension at p supplies a
finite supergradient alpha of phi. Hence, on the whole canonical body,

    f(z,X)<=f(p,y)+alpha.(z-p)+g.(X-y).                (18)

Now assume (p,y) is a GLOBAL buffered maximizer and (7) holds. Let I
be the set of bases of all global buffered maximizing points. Combine
its selected caps and weights from Section 4, and set

    A=sum_j rho_j a_j,        ell=A-epsilon alpha.

For any other buffered maximizing (z,X), each active quantile at (p,y)
imposes

    a_j.(z-p)+u_j.(X-y)<=epsilon[f(z,X)-f(p,y)].

Weight these inequalities and use (9),(18). The result is

    ell.(z-p)<=0.                                     (19)

Thus ell supports conv I at p. It vanishes on the minimal face F_p of
conv I containing p, because p lies in the relative interior of that
face. For EVERY z in F_p and EVERY X in C_z, the weighted actual cap
margin is

    sum rho_j[a_j.(z-p)+u_j.(X-y)+epsilon f(p,y)]
      =epsilon[f(p,y)+alpha.(z-p)+g.(X-y)]
      >=epsilon f(z,X)>=0.                            (20)

Consequently the same fixed closed caps (10) cover the whole actual
fiber over every such base, and in particular every integer fiber
whose base belongs to F_p. This proof does not use the invalid ordinary
claim that those caps pass through their assigned source, or that their
continuous normals sum to zero.

There is a precise nested-body extension. If C_t is a nested compatible
subfamily with the same positive sampled bases, its corresponding
buffer f_t is at most f on their common domain, by inclusion
monotonicity. On the OLD fixed face F_p, the same weighted margin
minus epsilon f_t is nonnegative by (18),(20). Thus those old quantile
thresholds still give a buffered cover there. This does NOT say that
the new deepest bases stay on the old face, nor that updating the
thresholds by one source's derivative preserves every contact
maximizer. Those are distinct continuation questions.

## 9. The projective-aligned power and its local normal circuit

For f=E^(1/(d+1)), (17) becomes the exact identity

    grad_y f=f a,

where a is the unique optimizing own-fiber projective parameter.
Thus the selected balance is

    sum rho_j u_j=epsilon f a.                         (21)

This has a useful algebraic interpretation wholly inside the source
fiber. Translate y to zero and use its positive projective chart
X'=X/(1+a.X). The own trace of (10) is u_j.X>=-epsilon f, which becomes

    (u_j-epsilon f a).X'>=-epsilon f.

The transformed continuous normals have EXACT weighted sum zero by
(21). Under the strict source-interiority condition (7) they are
nonzero: an inner source ball of radius r implies ||a||<1/r, while
epsilon f<r can be arranged by the same strict bound. This is an
ordinary local normal identity only; the integer bases and mixed
measure have NOT been projectively transformed.

For this power one may choose the full supergradient in Section 8
from a supergradient of F=E^(1/d), using f=F^(d/(d+1)). The proven
energy positive-chart theorem then gives

    1+a.(X-y)+(alpha/f).(z-p)>=1/(d+1)  on ALL of C.

In this particular choice the full tangent denominator is uniformly
positive; mere concavity of an arbitrary buffer would supply only a
nonnegative tangent. The supporting base work remains the actual
ell=sum rho a_j-epsilon alpha of (19). These facts align buffered
active normals with admissible global projective fields, but provide
no cap-loss or parity denominator payment by themselves.

## 10. Rigidity on the fixed face for the projective-aligned power

Continue with f=E^(1/(d+1)) and the minimal deepest-base face F_p in
Section 8. Every buffered maximizing point w=(z,X) with z in F_p
satisfies equality in the full supergradient inequality (18). Indeed
the weighted buffered constraints give a nonpositive value, while on
this face the same value is epsilon times the nonnegative tangent
deficit in (18). Their equality follows, and every positively weighted
individual constraint is also an equality.

Take any two such marked points and their segment. The convex region
D_(Q_epsilon,epsilon) contains the segment. The same argument forces f
to equal the one affine tangent at every point of that segment.
Write F=E^(1/d), so f=F^kappa with 0<kappa=d/(d+1)<1.
Concavity of F and STRICT concavity of the scalar power imply that
affinity of f along a nontrivial segment forces equal F at the
endpoints and equality in the joint F concavity inequality. By the
audited equality theorem for projective energy, the two entire marked
fibers are translations of one another, and the target fiber at each
intermediate base is exactly their marked Minkowski interpolation.
Strict inclusion could not preserve this equality.

In particular each selected base has a unique maximizing mark on
this face: two different marks in one bounded body cannot make its
centered translates identical. Taking convex combinations of the
marked points at vertices of F_p gives an affine marked graph on all
of F_p. Different convex representations of the same base give the
same mark by the just-proved uniqueness. Every real fiber on this
face is a translate of the same full-dimensional body, and all these
marked fibers have equal energy and equal volume.

This is rigidity on ONE minimal face associated with a buffered
maximizer. It is not a claim that all deepest bases belong to that
face, that the entire mixed family is a product, or that its mass is
exhausted by a bounded number of such faces. Supporting/nonregular
active caps are allowed in this rigidity argument; Section 6's
coarea identities were not used.

## 11. Affine normalization is a separate issue

The Euclidean buffer used above is a fixed-family construction. With
f=E^(1/(d+1)) and fixed epsilon it is neither invariant under arbitrary
fiber linear maps nor under continuous-coordinate scaling. No outer
affine-invariant minimizing-body argument is inferred from it.

There is a precise invariant variant. For the fixed original family
put

    Sigma=(1/M)sum_z |K_z| Cov(uniform K_z),
    Gamma_C(u)=sqrt(u^T Sigma u),
    f_hat=(E/M)^(1/(d+1)).

The within-fiber covariance Sigma is positive definite. Replace the
buffer in the unnormalized directional inequality by
epsilon f_hat(w) Gamma_C(u), and normalize Gamma_C(u)=1 instead of
||u||=1. All fixed-family compactness, convexity, and supergradient
proofs go through with this fixed ellipsoidal normal sphere. Its
normals remain bounded and bounded away from zero in Euclidean norm.

Under a lattice-preserving map

    z'=U z+z_0,      X'=A X+B z+c,

where U is an integer unimodular matrix and A is invertible, volumes,
E and M all acquire the common factor |det A|. Within-fiber covariance
transforms as Sigma'=A Sigma A^T. The transformed continuous covector
is u'=A^(-T)u, so Gamma_(C')(u')=Gamma_C(u), while f_hat is unchanged.
The cap margin transforms exactly by the corresponding base-covector
change. Thus this variant, including the normalized depth, is invariant
under these actual lattice-preserving coordinate maps. No projective
transformation of the base labels is used.

For regular active normal variations its section centroid is now

    bar z=p,
    bar X=y-epsilon f_hat grad Gamma_C(u),

because Euler's identity gives u.grad Gamma_C(u)=Gamma_C(u)=1.
The source balance remains sum rho u=epsilon grad f_hat. For this
power grad f_hat=f_hat a, so the local projective normal cancellation
still holds. When the BODY varies, however, Gamma_C varies as well:
the threshold derivative acquires the additional term
-epsilon f_hat dot Gamma_C(u), as well as the normalization derivative
in f_hat through M. Those terms must be retained in any physical
response calculation. Formula (15) or (17) is NOT silently imported
unchanged into this invariant variant.

## 12. Exact interval calibration of the buffered maximum

Take the actual product C=[-1,1]_z times [-1,1]_X, sampled at the
three integer bases -1,0,1. Thus M=6. For the length buffer f=T in
d=1 one has f(z,Y)=2(1-|Y|). Let 0<epsilon<1/2 and delta=2epsilon.
At (0,0), the own buffered trace has length 1+delta. The two endpoint
traces have opposite shifts before the common outward buffer, so
their lengths sum to at least 2. This follows directly by comparing
with the complementary unbuffered interval tails. Equality is attained
for every base tilt of absolute value at least 1+delta. Consequently

    Q_epsilon=3+2epsilon,

and (0,0) is the UNIQUE buffered deepest point. To check uniqueness,
at any (0,Y) choose the continuous sign facing Y and a sufficiently
steep base tilt. Its cap mass is

    3-|Y|+2epsilon(1-|Y|)
      =3+2epsilon-(1+2epsilon)|Y|.

At either extreme base, a steep base tilt isolates the own buffered
trace and gives an upper bound 1+2epsilon, strictly smaller. The
closed pure-base depth at (0,0) is 4, so it is not active.

Choose regular tilts a=2 and -2 when epsilon<1/2. The two actual
selected caps are 2z+X>=-delta and -2z-X>=-delta. Both have mass
3+delta. Their only proper sections are at base zero and coordinates
-delta and +delta, exactly (12). Their closed source traces cover the
entire middle interval. This calibration checks the distinction
between the actual original deepest mass 3 and the buffered mass
3+2epsilon; no original-depth gain is claimed.

## 13. A regular selected cap forces a singleton deepest-base face

This consequence applies to either the Euclidean fixed-family buffer
or its fixed ellipsoidal-normal version. Let (p,y) be a global buffered
maximizer satisfying the source-interiority condition (7), let F_p be
its minimal deepest-base face, and use the selected positive-weight
cap group and full supergradient from Sections 4 and 8. Suppose at
least ONE selected cap, of positive weight, is regular with respect
to all base-tilt parameters: its q-quantile is differentiable in a,
with derivative equal to its fixed mixed section barycenter bar z.
The full regularity in Section 6 is sufficient, but stronger than
necessary here.

Then F_p={p}.

Indeed, at the original maximizing point the cap is active and
feasibility of all base-tilt variations gives

    grad_a c_q(a,u)=p.

If (z,X) is any other buffered maximizing mark with z in F_p, the
weighted constraints used in Section 8 have nonpositive individual
values and weighted sum zero: their weighted sum is at least the
nonnegative full-supergradient deficit, while all constraints hold.
Every positive-weight cap is therefore active at (z,X) as well.
Its SAME quantile c_q(a,u), for the SAME original measure and the
SAME fixed normal parameters, now obeys

    grad_a c_q(a,u)=z

by feasibility of every base-tilt variation at this second maximizing
mark. Differentiability identifies z=p. If F_p were positive
dimensional, its vertices would include another deepest base; each
has a maximizing mark. This is a contradiction. Thus F_p is a point.

If every buffered maximizing base admits such a selected group, all
bases in I are extreme points of conv I. Moreover I is lattice-complete:
convexity of D_(Q_epsilon,epsilon) puts a maximizing actual mark at any
integer barycenter of its maximizing marked points. Two distinct
elements of I in the same parity class would have an integer midpoint
in I which is not extreme. Hence

    |I|=k(I)<=k(P)<=2^n.

Here k(I) is the vertex/witness number of I; all its points are extreme,
so it equals |I|. The monotonic witness bound k(I)<=k(P) is the same
archived finite-base bound used in the general fixed-face cover.

In this regular regime each group's finite contact minimum has one
base. This is a consequence of an attained regular buffered problem;
it is NOT obtained simply by approximating an arbitrary minimizer by
smooth fibers. Such an approximation need not preserve the required
variational stationarity, and no density argument is used here.

## 14. A concrete regular regime, without a minimizer approximation claim

For d>=2, if every sampled fiber is strictly convex, every nonvertical
cap mass is continuously differentiable in its full hyperplane parameters.
Here strict convexity means every supporting face consists of one point;
no smooth boundary or positive curvature is assumed. Thus at a buffered
maximizer with a proper own section the quantile is C1, its total coarea
is positive, and Section 13 applies to every selected cap group.

To see the regularity directly, on each fiber a proper section and its
first moment vary continuously under small changes of its cutting plane.
This follows, for example, by parametrizing nearby hyperplanes over the
old one: their convex sections converge in Hausdorff distance to the
proper section, which has interior in that hyperplane. Their (d-1)-volumes
and first moments consequently converge. At a limiting supporting plane,
strict convexity makes the limiting section a single point. Every sequence
of nearby nonempty sections has diameter tending to zero by compactness;
otherwise two separated limit points would belong to that supporting
face. Since d-1>0, their section measures and first moments tend to zero.
For strict full or empty cuts the same measures are zero locally. These
arguments are uniform along any convergent sequence of normal/threshold
parameters with the continuous normal bounded away from zero.

The elementary coarea derivative formula on the proper region therefore
extends continuously across supporting cuts with zero derivative. At an
exact supporting parameter, the volume between its plane and a nearby
plane is o(the parameter displacement): the affected points lie in an
O(displacement)-thick slab, and the supremum of its section areas tends
to zero by the preceding argument. This proves differentiability there,
including simultaneous normal and threshold changes. Summing the finite
fiber formulas proves the full cap regularity and the mixed section
barycenter formula. The proper own section makes the threshold derivative
strictly negative, so the implicit quantile derivative exists as claimed.

For d=1, supporting sections have H^0-measure one; endpoint jumps need
not disappear. This is why the stated regularity implication uses d>=2.
The separate supporting-directional inverse theorem treats all dimensions.

Finally, strict convexity is only a sufficient regularity condition for
an ACTUAL family. Approximating a general compatible minimizing family by
strictly convex fibers does not prove that an attained minimum remains in
that class, that all two-sided variations remain admissible, or that its
stationarity multipliers remain bounded. No such promotion is made here.
